rows.description: I see a stray dog thirsty in the heat and put out water. Small kindness to animals grows my heart, and I learn to be careful and tell an adult first.
I learn how a farmer grows my food and how a sweeper keeps streets clean. Respect for those who work with their hands makes me waste less and thank them.
I hear about climate change and become anxious about the future. That is understandable. I can talk to an adult and focus on small steps that are within my control.
I watch rain or a big tree and feel amazed. Wonder makes me want to protect nature, and simple things like planting a sapling connect me to it.

A teacher's kindness helped me through a dark year, and I feel deep thanks. Wise: gratitude can coexist with clear eyes; support the good, keep thinking. Harmful: feeling that thanks means never questioning.

My friend has cut off his family for the ashram and I worry about him. Wise: keep the door open, stay warm, ask curious questions, avoid attacking his teacher. Harmful: ultimatums that push him deeper.
Finds peace and direction in devotion; stays alert to signs of exploitation such as demands for money, isolation from family or suppression of questions.

I ask my teacher before every decision and feel lost without him. Wise: a good guide builds my judgement, not my dependence; make small choices alone and see that I can. Harmful: outsourcing my whole life.
I noticed something wrong earlier and said nothing, and now it is bigger. Wise: speak up now, acknowledge the delay, and let the facts lead. Harmful: staying silent because I already stayed silent.

I reported and nothing happened, and I feel cynical about all systems. Wise: try another channel, connect with groups that know the process, and keep some faith in change. Harmful: deciding nobody can be trusted.

After I reported an issue, my boss turned cold and colleagues stopped speaking to me. I feel punished for doing right. Wise: document retaliation, lean on outside support, and remember that integrity has costs and value.

I found evidence of fraud in my workplace and I am afraid of losing everything. Wise: keep copies safely, learn whistleblower protections, seek legal advice, and choose the safest right channel. Harmful: acting impulsively or leaking in anger.
Sometimes the older toddler hands a toy over to the crying baby and pats him: early empathy. Caregivers should notice and warmly name it, without demanding it every time.
The older child feels the baby gets everything and grabs to test whether he still matters. Parents should give one-on-one time and separate turns, not shame him as selfish.
Grabs back, shouts or bites; learns through adult labelling ("you are angry") that feeling is allowed but hitting is not.
The small one clutches the toy and screams, having no words for mine. Caregivers should step in gently, name the feeling, and offer another turn rather than forcing sharing at once.
My team follows my direction and thanks me and I feel proud yet unsure. I keep asking for honest feedback, share credit, and stay approachable so respect does not slide into fear or flattery.

I have just become manager over former peers and fear they think I don't deserve it. I am honest about what I don't know, listen more than I prove myself, and let results build authority rather than acting bossy.

Former peers who wanted the promotion are cool or sarcastic toward me and I feel hurt. I stay generous, acknowledge their strengths, give them meaningful work, and let time settle it rather than demanding warmth.

I feel lost as a new manager and hesitate to ask my own boss for help. Asking for coaching early is a strength; I bring specific problems and options, not just worry, and learn from more experienced leaders.
Others from my home community welcome me warmly, and I feel safe. Wise: enjoy the comfort while also making friends beyond it. Harmful: treating outsiders with suspicion.

People are polite but never invite me in, and my accent makes me feel like an outsider. Wise: keep showing up in clubs, classes and small talk; belonging is built slowly. Harmful: assuming all locals dislike me.

I miss home food, language and family and cry in secret. Wise: schedule calls, cook familiar meals, find fellow migrants, and know that it eases with time. Harmful: isolating or judging myself for missing home.

In a new city or country I fear making mistakes with language, food and rules. Wise: ask, watch, be patient with a learning curve, and find a small community. Harmful: staying only in a bubble that never lets me learn.
